question: An email claiming to be from PayPal is sent from "security@paypa1-alerts.com". What's the biggest red flag here?

options.text: The email address is too long
"paypa1-alerts.com" isn't PayPal's real domain
It uses lowercase letters
It has a subject line

explanation: Legitimate companies send email from their own real domain, not something that merely resembles it. "paypa1-alerts.com" (note the "1" standing in for an "l") isn't a PayPal domain at all.

question: An email says: "Your account will be suspended in 24 hours unless you verify now." What tactic is this?

options.text: Manufactured urgency
A legitimate security policy
Spam filtering
Two-factor authentication

explanation: A false deadline pressures you to act before you stop and think it through. Real account issues rarely come with a countdown timer.

question: A link displays as "www.yourbank.com", but hovering over it shows it actually points to "yourbank.verify-secure.ru". What should you do?

options.text: Click it — the displayed text says the right thing
Don't click it — the real destination doesn't match what's displayed
Click it in a private/incognito window to be safe
Reply to the email asking if it's real

explanation: The visible link text can say anything at all — what actually matters is where the link really goes. A mismatch like this is one of the clearest signs of phishing.

question: A suspicious email asks you to click a link to "confirm your identity." What's the safest way to actually check your account?

options.text: Click the link and log in as normal
Reply to the email with your username and password
Go to the real site directly by typing the address yourself, not through the email's link
Forward the email to a friend to ask their opinion

explanation: Navigating to the site yourself, or using a bookmark you already trust, sidesteps the fake link entirely — no need to guess whether a link is safe if you never click it.

question: Which of these is most likely a phishing lookalike domain, if the real bank is "chase.com"?

options.text: chase.com/login
online.chase.com
chase-security-alert.com
All of these are equally safe

explanation: "chase-security-alert.com" is a completely different, separate domain that just happens to contain the word "chase". Real Chase links always end in chase.com itself (or a subdomain of it, like online.chase.com) — never a separate lookalike domain.
